speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to establish a mechanism for the security of alimony payments in an estranged marriage, thus removing much of the anguish suffered primarily by mothers who frequently must spend time and money pursuing defaulting husbands and who often resort to welfare at immense cost in human terms as well as some $1 million daily in welfare costs. speechtext: I hope I can remember the question, Mr. Speaker. My question is addressed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. In view of the fact it is now over four months since the passage of the Foreign Investment Review Act, and in view of the fact there are still no legal ways to prevent takeovers that come within the ambit of that act, has the minister been successful in either delaying or freezing the completion of any takeover transactions which are reviewable? If so, how many takeovers has he prevented?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: DEGREE OF SUCCESS UNDER NEW LAW IN PREVENTING TAKEOVERS OF CANADIAN COMPANIES BY FOREIGN INTERESTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the two takeovers that have been of particular interest, the Masco takeover of Emco and the Reynolds takeover of Macdonald, have been under very considerable discussion. Neither was prevented because they both went through quite legally. However, both companies have given undertakings. In the case of Reynolds Tobacco, they are substantial undertakings and I think they substantially meet the significant benefit test. In the case of the Masco takeover of Emco, I am not yet satisfied that the undertakings given by that company, which are entirely voluntary, meet the significant benefit test. I have been told by senior officials of Masco that they will resubmit undertakings to us.

subsubtopic: DEGREE OF SUCCESS UNDER NEW LAW IN PREVENTING TAKEOVERS OF CANADIAN COMPANIES BY FOREIGN INTERESTS
speechtext: In view of the fact the Financial Times has reported up to 14 takeovers since the passage of the act, will the minister advise if he has any monitoring operation under way on an ongoing basis to check the actual number of takeovers taking place across the country in order to at least have control of the situation that has developed since the act was passed by the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: DEGREE OF SUCCESS UNDER NEW LAW IN PREVENTING TAKEOVERS OF CANADIAN COMPANIES BY FOREIGN INTERESTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have no special or legal monitoring system. Our sources of information are rather similar to the hon. member's. There is no legal obligation at the present moment for those involved in takeovers to advise the government of their intentions. I can say, however, that a large number of firms, maybe as many as 20, have come forward in conformity with the request I made last December to make us aware of their intentions, if they were contemplating a take-over, and to discuss the transaction with us.

subtopic: HEATING OIL PURCHASED BY GOVERNMENT FROM ROUMANIA

April 4, 1974

indicated that while the Canadian refineries could cover their requirements some of the importers would not be in a position to do so, and that action would need to be taken. subtopic: HEATING OIL PURCHASED BY GOVERNMENT FROM ROUMANIA

subtopic: HEATING OIL PURCHASED BY GOVERNMENT FROM ROUMANIA

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: HEATING OIL PURCHASED BY GOVERNMENT FROM ROUMANIA
speechtext: Does the minister regard it as appropriate for the government of Canada to do business on this scale with an advisor to the government? speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: HEATING OIL PURCHASED BY GOVERNMENT FROM ROUMANIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition may be misunderstanding the nature of the technical advisory group. All of the eastern Canadian refiners and the major importers of oil into eastern Canada were represented on that body, for the obvious reason that the committee was an important source of information for the government in regard to supply of oil to the eastern Canadian market and the demand that could be anticipated. All of the Eastern Canadian industry was involved in the discussions in this process and, in fact, if the government had not been pursuing this particular course of action to protect Canadians, there would have been no one else to deal with under these circumstances. The decision was made by myself on the advice of my officials. At no time was there a decision of the technical advisory group to enter into any specific transaction. They provided information and informed comment on the market. The decision was ours.

This amendment to the National Parks Act is significant in that it removes from the act the sort of special references to Indian lands which date back over a lengthy period in our history. At one time, Indian lands were regarded as lands belonging to the Crown and held in trust for the Indian people, but not as lands which belonged to them. That concept of Indian lands is increasingly becoming obsolete. Hopefully, it will be removed altogether from the Statutes of Canada. That is why I am happy that the House is willing to consent to this amendment to the National Parks Act, even though the amendment in some ways is symbolic. following:

He said: Mr. Speaker, these amendments are proposed because in committee there was elaborate consideration of a system of public hearings relative to the establishment of parks which have already been agreed upon with the provinces. I do not think it is advisable for members of parliament to create a situation in which they are likely to question the judgment of a provincial government, when a provincial government has decided to turn land over to the federal government for the establishment of a national park.
Members should be aware how parks are established, and how Crown lands in provinces which are available to provincial governments are turned over to the federal government so that national parks can be established within provinces. We must go to the provincial government and ask if it wants a national park in that province. If it does, the provincial government is responsible for assembling the land and transferring it to the federal government. Only then does the federal government step in. If a provincial government must expropriate lands, generally speaking we offer to pay 50 per cent of the cost of expropriation. The provincial government must decide if it wishes to place these lands in the hands of the federal government.
If we were to establish an onerous system of public hearings by which the judgment of provincial authorities could be questioned, we could jeopardize in many cases opportunities for Canadians to acquire more national parks. Of course, negotiations are entered into before land is turned over to the federal government. Agreement in
National Parks Act
principle is reached between the two governments. A system of public hearings in connection with a province's decision to establish a national park could force provincial authorities to reconsider their decision. I do not think it is up to us to question the decision of provincial authorities if they have decided to turn over lands to the federal government for the establishment of a national park. If we question their wisdom, I and any successor in my portfolio, might just as well forget about establishing national parks.
We have had a difficult experience in Nova Scotia. The public did not understand what was involved. It was decided at the provincial level that a national park should not be established if the public were against it. I do not think that the way the provincial government disposed of Crown lands was constitutionally proper. A case in Nova Scotia established very clearly that the system we have followed so far permits enough flexibility for a provincial government to change its mind before turning over land to the federal government. In the ship harbour case, there was agreement in principle between the federal government and the government of Nova Scotia to establish a national park in the Ship Harbour area. Apparently some people were not happy with that. I strongly disagree with the decision of the provincial government, and I stated this in strong words, to withdraw from that project because they feel it is not the best thing to do. I think the system has worked well. If we were to include in the act a provision to force the provincial governments to hold public hearings into all parks that have already been agreed upon, then what would the situation be?
We have 10 new national parks in Canada, seven of which were established in the provinces. The provinces are in the process of turning over or have already turned over these lands to the federal government. There is the case of the Pacific Rim National Park in British Columbia, Forillon and La Mauricie in Quebec, Gros Morne in Newfoundland, Kouchibouguac in New Brunswick and so on. The provinces have already acted on them and have turned over the land to the federal government. It would be most unwise at this time to have public hearings in order to question the wisdom of the provincial governments in deciding to establish these parks. I am quite at ease with the way things are now because there is no political coloration when dealing with the provinces about establishing parks. I have dealt with governments of all shades in the political spectrum of Canada.
When I negotiated for the Pacific Rim National Park, it was with a Social Credit government. In Ontario, I deal with a Tory government; in New Brunswick with a Conservative government and in Quebec with a Liberal government. In Newfoundland, I started negotiating with a Liberal government and now I am dealing with a Conservative government. In Nova Scotia, I deal with a Liberal government. I am now having discussions with regard to new national parks with the NDP governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
I do not want to cause any problems. I just want a proper mechanism that will protect something that is very important in Canada, the preservation of more acres of land for conservation purposes only. This is why I do not

April 4, 1974
National Parks Act
think it would be advisable to impose in clause 10 the mechanism of clauses 4 to 7 for parks already agreed upon by the federal and provincial governments. I think it would make it more difficult for any minister in this portfolio to create new national parks.
I would like to be precise and state the case. The members of my party have not agreed to these amendments. I think they are self-defeating for the purpose of establishing national parks. Clauses 4 to 7 have been included at the request of the official opposition and with the support of other members, but not from my party. I would like the people of Canada to know that we did not like clauses 4 to 7, but we accepted them because they were recommended by the committee. I would like to give a warning to anyone who is in favour of national parks in Canada that this mechanism would make it difficult for any minister to be as efficient as this government has been in establishing new national parks in Canada, 10 new national parks in four years when there were only four new national parks in the previous four years.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a few comments to this particular motion. The motion refers to striking out clauses 4 to 7 of the amendments put in during the committee hearings. Our party appreciates that this particular clause refers to parks which have been set aside and which, in effect, are a fait accompli. It is not our intention to put any obstacles in the way of the development of these parks. Far from it. Our sole purpose in moving the amendments in committee was to make the point that, with regard to any new parks that might be developed in the future, public hearings should be held to determine the feelings of the people, not only in the vicinity of the park but across Canada.
I appreciate that in most cases parks are developed by agreement between the provincial and federal governments. The provincial governments do a lot of soul searching. They have a lot of discussion before agreeing to turn over the land to the federal government to develop a park. We-feel, and this matter was discussed in committee, that possibly an amendment should be made to the act to grant a public hearing with regard to the development of a park in instances where the provincial government sets land aside without having a public hearing. Our point is simply that we believe that, in connection with the development of any new park, there should be a procedure for full and complete public hearings.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has tried to throw a red herring across the path of this House with his suggestion that this would somehow interfere with federal-provincial agreement on the creation of national parks. It was not the intention, nor will it be the effect of the amendment, that was accepted by the majority of the committee to question provincial judgment on matters respecting national parks.
The establishment of national parks in Canada is an important matter. The minister if asking this House to trust the judgment of two governments without any opportunity for citizenship participation, without any opportunity for individual people of Canada, whether they are affected directly, whether they are members of the national and provincial parks association of Canada or whether

they have any other reason to be interested, to make their views known relative to the boundaries, sites and related matters of new national parks that might be established.
I was amused to hear the minister suggest that the recent case in Nova Scotia somehow indicates there is an opportunity for individual Canadians to change decisions that are made in secret and in private by two levels of government. The best I can say for the minister's argument is that he is trying to make the best out of a very bad case. He knows as well as anyone else interested in parks in Canada that what happened in the case of Nova Scotia was a very exceptional and sad case in the history of the development of national parks in Canada. The reason the Liberal government of Nova Scotia caved in on the Ship Harbour national park was that there had been allowed to develop a substantial suspicion about it, a suspicion that was engendered precisely because there was no opportunity at the time when changes could have been made for the people directly affected to themselves make a case, express their concern and have some influence on the decision before it was made.
What the amendments accepted by the committee achieved is assurance that citizens will have a right to review decisions respecting national parks before they are a fait accompli. That is what was done. It was an attempt to assure to individual Canadians the right to question and perhaps improve upon decisions taken in secret by two levels of government. The amendment put before the committee, and accepted by the committee, would not have resulted in protracted discussion or debate which would have delayed interminably the establishment of new national parks. Provision was made for a limited period during which public hearings would be held. What the minister is concerned about here is simply an invasion upon the preserve which he and his officials have enjoyed exclusively for far too long. They have become accustomed to making these decisions in isolation without reference to the people of Canada, either those particulary interested because they live in areas where parks might be established, or those who might be concerned because of their particular interest in conservation.
The minister did make a concession. He allowed an amendment which would provide for a public hearing at such time or times as he, the minister, considered appropriate. Anyone who is experienced in this field knows that such an undertaking is virtually useless. It means that hearings will be held after the decisions have been taken. We have all had experience with that sort of thing. What the minister is offering in the amendment which he introduced, and which he has allowed to stand, is simply an opportunity for individual citizens to express their opinions, not to effect any changes.
Mr. Speaker, there are two kinds of public hearings. There is the public hearing which is designed to acquaint people with what has been done-that is a public relations hearing-and there is the public hearing which is allowed to influence what is going to be done. That is participation, and it is a useful kind of hearing. What the minister is trying to prevent, in the amendment now before us, is participation. He is all in favour of a public relations hearing which would allow citizens to become involved
April 4, 1974

when there is no point in their being involved. No opportunity would be afforded to conservationists or other interested groups to affect decisions which concern the location of national parks.
In testimony before the committee the minister was quite explicit on this point. He left no doubt as to his intention to shut the people of Canada out when it came to decisions on these matters. Of course, the original decisions have to be taken in private between the federal government and the province concerned, or between the federal government and the territory. But after the decisions have been taken, there should be an open public hearing. There are two reasons why this should be so. One is based on principle: there is a legitimate public interest in public business. The second reason is that continued privacy does not work. The system which the minister and his officials wish to perpetuate has created problems which public hearings could have avoided.
The best evidence of this concerns the proposed new park in the Yukon, Kluane. When the standing committee was in Whitehorse, we heard two concerns expressed by people who, before the arrival of the committee, had been given no public opportunity to discuss these matters arising from the establishment of a major new national park in their territory. The first concern was that no adequate survey of resources had been carried out, and that this failure to make an adequate survey might lead, later, to the disruption of the park. The second point was that there had been an inadequate explanation of the reasons which led the minister, after a discussion with mining companies, apparently in secret, to exclude 2,000 square miles of land originally scheduled for inclusion in the park. There was also the question of native rights, a question which had not been publicly aired prior to the arrival in Whitehorse of the standing committee.
I should like to put this question to the minister and to all Canadians who are concerned about national parks: whose interest is served when the size of a park is cut in secret by a minister meeting with representatives of mining interests in the north? Is the interest of the National and Provincial Parks Association served by a secret decision of this kind arrived at in the course of a meeting between a politician and representatives of mining interests? Is the general interest of the public served? Are the interests of the people of the Yukon served? Of course not. All these interests would be much better served if there were public hearings along the lines of the amendment we were able to introduce, and which was carried in the committee-an amendment which the minister is now trying to strike down.
I ask again: whose interest is served when a park is established without any serious effort being made to determine the hydro or resource potential which exists within its limits? I ask you to assume for a moment, Mr. Speaker, that a later generation happens to find a bonanza within the area of Kluane National Park, a bonanza similar to that which might have already been found had adequate surveys been carried out. If this bill stands and the minister's way prevails, mining interests in that later generation might also hold secret meetings with a future minister, meetings of the kind the hon. gentleman opposite has held with developers, and such meetings might result
National Parks Act
in a reduction of the land set aside in Kluane. More than the situation at Kluane would be affected, because once the process of excision begins in one park, no national park is safe. Parks would be endangered not only in the Yukon, but in all the provinces and territories of Canada. This is an aspect which all hon. members should consider before they cast their votes today on the minister's attempt to secure an amendment which would preserve this right to make secret decisions in areas of public business.
To return to the example the minister gave. Whose interest was served by so much secrecy and high-handedness in connection with Ship Harbour National Park, circumstances which led to the proposal for that park being cancelled and withdrawn? The secret procedures followed by the minister led to a situation in which Nova Scotia is without a national park at Ship Harbour. It was the purpose of myself and my colleagues on the committee to establish a procedure applicable to future parks, as well, but we were advised that an amendment along those lines would have gone beyond the ambit of the bill, that the unanimous consent of the House would have been necessary if it were to be accepted. And having looked at the minister's track record, we anticipated that the minister would not have agreed. So, in the circumstances, we sought to establish this principle in the case of the parks designated in the schedule to the bill, as well as those at Kluane, Nahanni, and on Baffin Island.
Certain valuable effects would follow if the House were able to uphold the judgment of the all-party standing committee and defeat the minister's attempt to undo the work of that committee. In future, when national parks are to be established or enlarged, a period of 90 days would be used for the purpose of determining whether special circumstances exist and, if there are problems, how serious they are likely to be. We would then be able to proceed on the basis of knowledge. The minister prefers to proceed as he did at Kluane, without holding public hearings and without telling anybody why 2,000 square miles were cut away. The minister did not even bother to find out what resource potential there might be which at a future time might mean a further large acreage being cut away from the park, setting a precedent which would endanger all national parks in Canada.
That is one result that would follow if we used the public hearings procedure. A second result that would follow is that it would provide a forum for the defenders of national parks, either of a park in that particular location or of national parks generally, to allay fears that might naturally develop. Had that been done at Ship Harbour, I venture to say that we would have had a new national park in Nova Scotia now. But we lost it because of the secrecy practised by the minister, which he now attempts to enshrine in legislation by these amendments today.
A third result that would follow is that we would inform more people about the importance of national parks. If the minister believes that his case for national parks in Canada has been won, that there is now a majority who in a given situation would prefer park development as opposed to resource development, then he is naive. Those

April 4, 1974
National Parks Act
of us who believe in national parks in Canada have a great selling job to do, and public hearings, as has been demonstrated on other occasions, can provide us with an opportunity to do that job.
A fourth effect of public hearings of the kind we are proposing, and which the minister is now trying to undo, is that we would establish the principle that our national parks are public business, that the government trusts the people enough to heed their voice in regard to where parks should be established and where their boundaries should be.
I, myself, proposed in the committee one procedure for public hearings, a procedure drawn from federal practice. The members of the committee felt that the procedure I proposed was too cumbersome, and I did not argue with that because I was interested in the principle of public hearings, not in their particular form. I was interested in their having an effect at a time that would allow people to have some influence on what was going to be done, instead of simply casting a useless vote yea or nay. I did not dig in on the question of the particular form of the public hearings I proposed. Instead, I accepted the language that had been proposed by my colleague from the NDP, the hon. member from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), language which the minister now proposes to strike down.
By their nature, national parks interest a minority of Canadians, although they are people who are genuinely concerned about our parks. They care deeply about the preservation of wild and natural places, and about the safety and protection of rare species and places. Those Canadians who want new national parks want these parks deeply. So, I believe, do the majority of the members of this House of all parties. The members of my party want them so much that we did literally everything in our power to have this bill passed in January rather than April. Before we agreed to an adjournment of this House, we insisted as a condition of that agreement that this bill be brought back at this stage so we could proceed immediately to pass it.
The minister disagreed and delayed the bill. The reason he did so, on the evidence of his amendments, is that the minister wants more than parks. This minister wants parks, the absolute control of which rests with him and his advisers, his bureaucrats. The difference between us on this bill and these amendments is that the minister wants authoritarian control over the parks. We want parks established by democratic procedures. The minister does not want to be bothered with parliament or with public hearings. He does not want to be bothered with territorial governments or with the National and Provincial Parks Association. He is, of course, prepared to consult with them, on his own terms and in his own time, but he is not prepared to give parliament or the public the right to participate, in an effective way, in a decision about where parks should be established, or how, or even why.
When this bill was first introduced in the other place, it did not even contain a requirement for public notice. It allowed the government to negotiate in secret any additions to parks and then to proclaim them without notice. It proposed to give to government the power to shut out of the process people whose land and lives might be affected, the conservation groups who might be interested and, of

course, to shut out the parliamentary process. But that provision was too strong even for the other place. There is a greater sense of democracy in the Senate than in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development so far as parks are concerned, because the other place amended the original bill and wrote in the requirement for a 90-day notice and publication in the Canada Gazette. That was the first change toward democratizing the procedure for setting up parks, and was a change that was forced on the minister.
Then, in the standing committee, other changes were proposed and passed to ensure that the public, from the poorest native with a trap line to the most sophisticated conservationist, would not be shut out of the process of establishing national parks. In particular, the committee required that the notice be published in various popular media, not buried in the fine print of the Canada Gazette. It established a process to guarantee public hearings at a period when proposals could still be changed, not hearings after the fact, as has been the practice of the minister, and as is his desire in the amendments that he is putting before the House today.
The committee voted deliberately to ensure that when parks are created in the two northern territories, the elected representatives of those territories would have a power stronger than the power of a mere rubber stamp. While our party initiated that idea, the amendment which carried was proposed by my colleague from Comox-Alberni, the hon. member of the NDP, and we will look forward when the voting comes to his support for the measure he proposed.
Throughout its deliberations the committee voted and acted against secrecy. It voted and acted to establish a system of parks by a democratic process. The amendments of the minister are designed to strike down those advances and to return to a situation where parks policy is decided by a select and secret few without any apparent trust in the people. That is a most alarming suggestion on the part of the minister and a most dangerous amendment. It places us back in the days when it was felt by governments, of all stripes perhaps, that the public had no rights. We believe that the public does have rights on questions of importance, such as the establishment of national parks, and consequently we intend to oppose the amendments moved by the minister which would deny the public the opportunity of playing a role in deciding questions concerning national parks while there was still a chance to influence those decisions.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark), with his usual eloquence, was discussing amendments 3 and 4, and since we are going to be voting on them together, I presume he was in order in doing so. It is not my intention to defend the minister from any of the attacks made upon his desire for extreme secrecy. I am sure the minister is capable of presenting his own case on that score. Nor is it my intention to try to go around and around again on some of the matters which went around and around for some time in the committee.
May I say at once that in my view the committee that dealt with this bill devoted itself with a great deal of diligence to trying to examine and to sort out a good many
April 4, 1974

complex issues that are inherent in this particular bill. I think it is fair to say that at the outset, when the bill was introduced in the other place, the minister, and probably his departmental officials, hoped the bill would be treated somewhat as a kind of housekeeping measure, to tidy up the situation and to put the final seal of parliamentary approval on the establishment of certain new national parks. Despite some of his criticisms about what happened at Ship Harbour, I think the hon. member for Rocky Mountain would not be averse to agreeing, at least to some extent, that the minister has devoted himself with some diligence to widening the national parks system in Canada. While there are many matters on which I may be in disagreement with the minister at this and other times, I am certainly quite prepared to give him some marks for his effort in this regard.
As I see it, there are essentially three important aspects to this bill, two of which are referred to in the two report stage amendments we are discussing in respect of Clauses 10 and 11 of the bill, and a third, which is not up for discussion at this time, covering provisions in Clause 2 of the bill for the governor in council to take steps leading to the addition of lands to existing parks. If you have noted the reprint of the bill you will have observed that there are certain additions to the original draft of the bill, incorporated in Clause 2, which apparently are not under debate or question at this time because no report stage amendments have been submitted to them. In point of fact the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) made some reference to these additions in Clause 2, in part at least. If I may say as an aside, they do represent what I consider to be an interesting development inasmuch as there is some automatic provision in that proposal for consideration by the standing committee and for action forthwith by the House on the report by the committee.
The hon. member for Rocky Mountain spent most of his time talking about this question of public hearings, and I think quite rightly said his party put certain proposals forward in respect of public hearings which have not emerged in the bill as reported from the committee. He was quite right when he said that. The additions to Clause 10, with which the report stage amendment proposes to deal, are in terms which I proposed originally on Clause 2 as accepted by the committee. I fully admit that at the point in time when this particular matter was under consideration, it was with the tacit agreement of members of the NDP who were on the committee that this addition be made to Clause 10 and part of it to Clause 11.
One of the important constitutional issues involved in Clause 10, and I think this fact should not be lost on this House in light of the remarks by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain, is the question of transfer of jurisdiction of lands within the provinces to the Crown in the right of Canada. Under the terms of the national parks trust, unless some future parliament undoes what parliament does at a given time, those lands remain forever in the status which parliament has assigned to them as national parks for the enjoyment of future generations of Canadians in unimpaired condition.
I do not quarrel too much with the argument put forward by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain, and also
National Parks Act
put forward very eloquently in the committee by his colleague the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), about the desirability of public hearings into the question of the establishment of parks. I hope his eloquent remarks today, and during some of the discussions that took place before the committee, will not fall on deaf ears so far as the governments of the provinces are concerned. As I said, if I recall correctly the lengthy discussions we had in trying to sort this thing out, at the point in time an approach is made by the federal government to a province for certain lands to be put into national parks, and at the point of time when a provincial government is prepared seriously to consider that proposal, or if indeed the provincial government were to decide to take some initiative to offer certain land to national parks, it would be very desirable that the government of the province initiate and hold the kind of hearings to which the hon. member for Rocky Mountain referred. It is very unfortunate that the government of Nova Scotia did not see fit to take that kind of action in respect of the Ship Harbour proposal at an earlier stage than the point in time at which it apparently decided to abandon it.
In the matter of the establishment of new parks in the provinces, that is the point in time, and I agree strongly with the hon. member for Rocky Mountain, that public hearings should be held into the advisability of there being created within that provinces, and from the lands of that province, a national park which would be surrendered to the people of Canada forever for that specific purpose. There is no way in which we in this House or this parliament can impose a provision of that kind upon the governments of the provinces. I do not have any regret that the hon. member for Rocky Mountain and his colleagues in the committee stressed this question of the need for public hearings so vigorously. But when one attempts to sort out all the complex issues involved, and I say this in spite of the fact that I was a party to this becoming part of the bill reported back to the House, then I must say I am now prepared to support the minister's report stage amendment.
I am not regretful in any way that we are having this report stage debate on this subject, and I am not regretful in any way that the minister was pushed to the point where he has to lay this kind of issue on the table, because hopefully the minister, in negotiating with the provinces, will pass on to them some of the views which are apparent among members of the House of Commons from all provinces regarding this matter of public hearings. My reaction might have been different under other circumstances, but I am glad the minister is not in his report stage amendment seeking to delete sub-clause (3). He is, as a result of the initiative of members of the Conservative party at the committee, leaving in that provision which requires the minister-and it says "shall"-to hold hearings on the question of how the park is to be used once it is officially established. I consider that to be a major improvement to the legislation as it was introduced. I think that in the context of the committee debates it should be apparent that the credit for initiating that particular idea during the committee proceedings rests with the hon. member for Rocky Mountain and his colleagues.

April 4, 1974
National Parks Act
The situation with reference to clause 11, which deals with the parks in the Territories, is of course quite different constitutionally to that which applies to the provinces because there the land is held in the right of the federal Crown. Normally, for administrative purposes, this land is under the authority of the Territorial Lands Act which act, in addition to the National Parks Act, I think is one which gives the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) responsibility. So, in the case of the Northwest Territories, the minister simply is saying that, as Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, he wishes to take that land from his jurisdiction under the Territorial Lands Act and propose that it be put under the National Parks Act. I think the minister can be cited for a lack of adequate public hearings on the question of advisability of establishing those parks. This is a matter of debate. However, all that clause 11 does is propose that three specific parks be added to the schedule of the National Parks Act.
So far as I know, the only public hearings that were held on the question in the sense the term is being used by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain were the public hearings held by the committee. That was one reason I strongly supported the idea of the committee going to Whitehorse, so we could at least learn the views of the people of the Yukon Territory. We had before the committee in Ottawa spokesmen interested in the various aspects of the proposed parks in the Northwest Territories. That process has taken place. There is information contained in the records of the committee which satisfies me that the councils of the two Territories had in fact approved the idea of these parks and that there is agreement on all questions except that of the rights of the aboriginal inhabitants of the area. Although there are other aspects of the territories in the north which will come up under one of the other report stage amendments, which I shall not go into at this point, it seems to me that this idea of having further committee hearings, which the deletion of the proposed section would call for, would be really rather redundant at this point in respect of the three specific parks proposed for the two territories.
So far as I am concerned this is not something which should really concern us too much. The minister at this point in effect is saying that we do not need committee hearings to examine these three particular parks in the territories. I really wish that the clauses of the bill which have to do with additions to existing parks had referred to the establishment of new parks. This relates to something the hon. member for Rocky Mountain said. This is beyond the scope of the bill but if that proposal had been included, along with the proposed committee amendments to clause 2 of the bill, then we would have had the other side of the coin. If there were a proposal to establish, either in the territories or in the provinces, a new national park, the standing committee of this House could examine the merit of the proposal, hopefully concurrent with public hearings held under arrangements made by the provinces or in the case of the territories hopefully through some arrangements made by the standing committee with the territorial councils. I think the status of the territories is a matter being discussed not very far

away from this chamber this afternoon by the committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I might have something to say about this later on when we come to one of the other report stage amendments, but so far as I am concerned the really important improvements that it was possible for the committee to make will be retained if the report stage amendments as introduced today are accepted by the House. I hope that, without too lengthy discussion by other members of the House, it may be possible for us to achieve the purpose that has been referred to by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain so eloquently; that is, a desire to have these particular parks which are to be finally established by this bill come into being for the benefit and use of the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, right at the outset I wish to indicate I am disappointed the minister has assumed this posture this afternoon. He has been in charge of the national parks program for a number of years. I think that anyone who has the privilege of this responsibility learns as his first lesson in the area of national parks administration that the essence of wisdom is communion with public opinion and having close rapport with the needs of the people of Canada. This is the reason, following the deliberations of the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the amendments were first proposed that there be close consultation with the people in all respects and this is why the amendments were approved at that time. I am sure the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) who just concluded his remarks, and who was with us in this viewpoint at that time, if he reconsidered the statements he has made, would come to the conclusion that his original wisdom was the correct approach.
The minister, in his statement this afternoon, has spoken once again about the marvellous developments that have taken place in the Canada national parks system in the past few years. I would remind the hon. gentleman that it has taken an unconscionably long time to achieve this breakthrough in the development and expansion of our national parks system. The amazing thing is that the public pressure for national parks has been growing, and under an atmosphere of that kind it should be relatively easy to have fairly substantial tracts of land reserved in order to meet the rising demand for recreational facilities and for the conservation and preservation of areas of particular interest in Canada. Notwithstanding the growing demand in the face of population pressures, in the face of more leisure time and also more disposable income, it has taken almost 20 years to make a major breakthrough in the development of national parks.
The bill that is before us now is the climax of negotiations that have been going on ever since the department of northern affairs and national resources was established in 1953. The minister at that time was the Hon. Jean Lesage, and he immediately began negotiations for the expansion of the national park system which has been carried on by succeeding governments. There had been hardly any development in the conservation area for a couple of decades previous to that time. The war, of course, interfered with developments at this time, and it was not until a depart-
April 4, 1974

ment was established that was specifically dedicated to the proposition of northern and resource development that we began to move in a positive direction.
Therefore, I am disappointed that the minister who has the responsibility for the department at the moment is reversing the approach that has gradually unfolded as the sensitive negotiations that have been going on for this long period have made it possible now to legislate some specific park areas into being.
I know that the initial breakthrough came in the latter 1950's and early 1960's with Terra Nova in Newfoundland, and also with a new national park in the province of Nova Scotia. The Maritimes have always been more responsive to national park development because long ago they recognized that one of their major assets was the natural beauty with which they are endowed. It was, therefore, fairly easy to persuade the Maritime provinces, particulary Nova Scotia when it was under the leadership of the hon. gentleman who is now the Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), to co-operate in the national parks development. He had a great sensitivity to the prospects of national park development in the interests of the general economy. Let me state as an aside that it was also in Nova Scotia that one of the major historic park developments was negotiated between the federal and the provincial governments, namely the complete restoration of the historic Fort Louisbourg which is now almost completed. That was also in the time of the provincial leadership of the hon. gentleman who is now leading the opposition in this House.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Other than the Maritimes, it has always been difficult to get provincial approval for a national park development. For example, when the first minister of the department of northern affairs and national resources, the Hon. Jean Lesage, became premier of the province of Quebec he became interested immediately in making available large tracts of land in that province which would become a part of the national parks system.
The two great areas of underdevelopment in the national parks system have been in the two major provinces- Ontario and Quebec. They preferred to develop their own provincial park systems rather than to work under the umbrella of the national parks system. I know from my own experience that one of the reasons they were so sensitive to federal intrusion was Ottawa's refusal to consult and negotiate in public, which is the posture that the minister is reverting to under the amendments which are before the House this afternoon. Unfortunately, the negotiations with the province of Quebec were delayed because of the "quiet revolution" that took place when the matter of federal-provincial jurisdiction became one of the major political concerns in the decade of the 1960's. Quebec has now established some national parks; Ontario still has a long way to go.
I suggest to the minister, who is not here at the moment-I trust that he will read my remarks-that he will not help to persuade Ontario to become an enthusiastic supporter of the national parks system if he reverses the trend that has been under way, particularly since the Resources for Tomorrow Conference, since the establish-
National Parks Act
ment of the Federal-Provincial Parks Association, and particularly since the establishment of the Resource Ministers Council which brought a new era of mutual understanding and concern in the conservation area. The refusal to consult in public, both with the governments and the people concerned, will hamper to a substantial degree the improved atmosphere that I am sure still prevails and the more positive attitude that prevails in the province of Ontario.
The proposal that is being made here this afternoon in the minister's amendments will make it extremely difficult to negotiate in the north. The new department of northern affairs and national resources for the first time brought that huge northern expanse of territory into the Canadian body politic in the early 1950's. Immediately negotiations got under way with a view to establishing a park in each of the territorial areas, in the Yukon territory, and in the western and eastern parts of the Northwest Territories. Ottawa, of course, had complete jurisdiction over the land area in the territory north of the 60th parallel, so the government of Canada could take quite an arbitrary approach in setting aside lands for the establishment of national parks.
Northerners are a very independent breed of frontiersmen and pioneers, and they made it quite clear that they wanted to have a say in how the land area of northern Canada should be used. Proposals have been under discussion with the various interests in the territories for a considerable number of years, and now they are coming before the House as legislation. They are still not finalized. The amendment before the House flies in the face of the experience of the committee when it met in the Yukon last December to consult with the local people with respect to the establishment of Kluane National Park. It was as a result of the direct contact of the members of the committee with vox populi as we discovered it during the two days of hearings at Whitehorse, that amendments were introduced to the legislation and approved by the committee. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) certainly felt, after hearing the expression of public opinion, that it was absolutely necessary that the process of consultation be extended. As a result, following the hearings in the Yukon, the committee approved these amendments.
Mr. Speaker, it is not going to ease the situation to reverse ourselves in this respect; indeed, I hope parliament will not do that and I hope that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni will stay with his original viewpoint. It was fresh in his mind when he first supported the amendment to broaden consultation. I guess after two or three months he has forgotten the forcefulness of public opinion in the territories on this matter. I suggest that he present himself to the committee that is now meeting in another part of parliament hill and listen to the representations by the spokesmen of the territorial governments.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member says he would be there if he did not have to listen to me. I do not order the business of this House, and I think it is unfortunate that members of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development are occupied with this debate this afternoon when they should be listening to the representations

April 4, 1974
National Parks Act
of members of the Northwest Territories and Yukon Councils who are in the city. My point is that if the hon. gentleman would listen to that voice once again and get tuned in to it he would not reverse himself as he indicated he was going to do in supporting the amendment proposed by the minister.
I understand the problem of the minister and the conflict of interest that is built into his portfolio. Northern development is actually opposed to the conservation interests. This conflict has always existed in the department, even when it was called northern affairs and resources. There were two aspects of that portfolio that had to be administered by the one minister. He had to assure development of the north and, at the same time, he had the conservationist responsibility under the resources aspect of his portfolio. The dichotomy is even more severe today and more difficult to reconcile because the department now emphasizes northern development which accentuates areas of economic development responsibility. It used to be merely northern affairs and this did not imply any particular emphasis. I am sure this problem cannot be reconciled until the minister is relieved of his responsibility in the area of resource conversation, and particularly in the area of administration of national parks.
I believe that national parks, in all their various manifestations, should come under the jurisdiction of the Department of the Environment. I trust that one of the major changes that will be made in the set-up of government departments will be in this area. I am sure that in the ministry of environment, the minister responsible will be only too pleased to consult with the people of Canada because no conservation program can be successful until it has the broad support of public opinion.
The vast majority of Canadians are now strongly in favour of wise management and multiple use of our renewable resources. National parks are in the area of renewable resources and, as the National Parks Act says, they should be kept in their original unspoiled state for the use of succeeding generations.
When it comes to consultation, the minister blows hot and cold, particularly in regard to national parks in western Canada which, like northern Canada, originally had the greatest acreage dedicated to the perpetual use of the people. That was because of the constitutional situation, of course, which provided that western lands areas were originally under the jurisdiction of the federal Crown, even as the northern land areas are under the jurisdiction of the federal Crown up to the present day. But national parks in western Canada increasingly have had to meet growing demands for multiuse of land areas in Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief because I only want to explain the purpose of this amendment.
I think there were lengthy discussions in committee to determine the kind of consultation that should take place both with the Council of the Yukon and the Council of the Northwest Territories with respect to the establishment of national parks in the north. After major discussions on the meaning of the words and the interpretation of the Department of Justice, I find I must ask the House to replace the words "approval by the Council" by the words "consultation with the Council" because the term "approval" actually means laying out a right for the Council of the Northwest Territories and the Council of the Yukon, or some sort of a right of veto over the administration of Crown lands in the north and it is not appropriate to discuss that matter here in this House when dealing with parks. If hon. members want to transfer the control of northern resources to the elected representatives of northern Canada, it will have to be done under another piece of legislation introduced before the House and now being considered in committee, the bill on the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories Administration.
With respect to clause 11, it would not be appropriate to change the very nature of Crown relations regarding land north of the 60,h parallel. That is why we decided to put back in the words "after consultation" because I think it is a question of eligibility since "approval" would give the elected representatives of the Northwest Territories constitutional powers not provided for under the Northwest Territories and Yukon legislation.
For this reason, Mr. Speaker, the government decided to re-establish the word "consultation" and if hon. members wish to submit the control of Canada's northern resources
April 4, 1974

to the approval of the representatives of the Territories, they should do it before the committee or during the consideration of the bill on the constitutional status of the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, seconded by my colleague from Hamilton East (Mr. Munro), I move that Motion No. 5 be adopted by the House.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not take much of the time of the House. The minister is proposing a return to the original language of the bill, language which in the considered judgment of the committee was inappropriate, language which the committee acted to strike out, to amend. The original language would have written into law a statutory double standard. It provided that if you wanted to establish a national park in Quebec, you must ask the local government; if you wanted to establish a national park in Ontario, you must ask the local government; but if you wanted to establish a national park in the Yukon or Northwest Territories, you tell the local government. Provisions like that make a mockery of any claim of belief in more self-government for the territories. We, in my party, do not propose to pass a mockery into law.
The minister has made the point that this matter can be discussed in committee during study of another bill. The point remains. There is language in the bill before the House today with which we, as a parliament, must deal today, in considering this bill. It is language in this bill, not in any other, which expresses the attitude of the House of Commons of Canada on the status and potential of governments in the territories of the north. You cannot get around this by saying that it should be dealt with in another bill. If this should be discussed during the consideration of another bill, the minister should not have introduced the word "consultation" into the present bill. He did. It is that with which we are dealing. A principle is involved which, although it might arise on other occasions and in other bills, has arisen here and cannot be blinked away.
Actually, it is known to members of the committee that there has been agreement by the councils for the particular parks established. There is no threat to them. What we are doing is establishing the attitude of parliament, the view of parliament, that there should be an increase in the powers of self-government existing in the northern territories. We also think that this bill would set a precedent for the establishment of future parks, so that if more parks are to be established in the north there must be approval by the elected representatives of the people and not merely some kind of consultation.
We, in the Progressive Conservative party, introduced an amendment which would, for the limited and special purposes of establishing national parks, give the people of the territories the same rights as the people of Ontario, Quebec and other parts of Canada, an amendment which would treat them as citizens not as subjects. Instead of consultations, we proposed that there must be the agreement of the elected councils of the territories before any large part of a territory could be taken away and used as a national park.
National Parks Act
My colleague from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), a member of the NDP, preferred a gentler word than agreement. He preferred "approval", an amendment requiring that the elected territorial councils approve of any proposal to permanently remove lands from an area that will soon be a province. We accepted his softer language. It expressed the principle that democracy means something in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. So, the amendment approved in committee is an amendment in the language of the NDP, and it is that which the minister proposes to strike down today. We oppose that action by the minister, that strike against democracy, and will look forward, when the voting comes, to having the support of the NDP in sustaining an improvement which the NDP itself proposed.
It is apparent to me, sir, that the minister and his advisers find it inconvenient to treat the people of the territories as though they are citizens. The minister and his advisers concocted a phony argument in committee, that to give the councils of the territories a say on whether a national park is to be established in this region is somehow to give them absolute control over all the natural resources of the north. That, sir, is an absurd argument, which ignores the very special nature of national parks. I, as the representative of a constituency with national parks in it, have every reason to know that when a national park is created, all manner of administrative problems are created too: Native rights are affected; normal jurisdiction over municipal highway and other matters is suspended or changed; planning becomes very difficult. That is evident in Alberta and wherever else national parks exist. The establishment of a national park very much alters and affects the future of the region in which the park lies. The word "consultation" would mean that the territories concerned would have no right to influence that territory's future direction. "Approval" would at least allow for a chance to shape that future.
Sir, the larger question of resources is not affected at all. Elected spokesmen of the territories have made it clear that the status they want is a status-I quote Ken MacKinnon of the Yukon Territorial Council, in testimony to the standing committee in Whitehorse in December:
Without the immediate control of natural resources, the reason being that we think we have to prove to the people of Canada and to the government of Canada that we are as capable of dealing with the resources of the province as any other area of Canada.
So, there is no question at all about control of resources.
There is, however, sir, a basic question which must be faced, the question as to whether we are going to trust the judgment of Canadians who happen to live in the two territories. Are we going to say that when it comes to establishing parks we trust the premier of Quebec more than we trust the elected representatives of the Yukon; that we trust the premier of Ontario more than the elected representatives of the Northwest Territories; that we trust the premier of Nova Scotia more than the duly elected representatives of the north? That is what it comes down to. Perhaps it is a hard question, because so much land is involved. I remind the House that there is also a lot of land in the north of several provinces, and while it might be inconvenient for the minister and his advisers to have to deal with elected representatives in the province before taking land away forever and creating a national park, we

April 4, 1974
National Parks Act
put up with that inconvenience because we are a democratic state. The amendment here, by the minister and his advisers, would have democracy stop at the border of the territories, so far as national parks are concerned.
The real question facing us is: Are we prepared to endorse that double standard and write it into law, or will we extend to the citizens of the territories the same trust on the limited question of national parks that we extend to the citizens of the rest of Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I wish to make a few comments on my position on this matter. I wish to make it clear that my position is not influenced by the semantics of the minister or the rhetoric of the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark). As the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) stated, an amendment was proposed in committee to substitute the words "consultation with" by the words "agreement had been reached with". We got into quite a discussion about what was involved in the legal meaning of the word "agreement". As the hon. member for Rocky Mountain said, I suggested that the words that might be used would be "following approval by".
The minister still maintains the position that somehow or other this would give the council of the territories legal power over the resources of the north. I am not going to argue that point with him now, but I would like to state briefly to the House my view of the position. We are looking at the text of a bill which is hopefully moving toward becoming the law of Canada. In this clause we are dealing with a proposal to establish three parks in the Northwest Territories. I stated in committee, and I still maintain at this time in history, that regardless of what should be done about changing the constitutional position of the two territories, under the bill that is being considered today, national parks should not be established in the Northwest Territories without the approval of the council.
According to the records of the committee, and the testimony given by people in Whitehorse with regard to these three specific parks, the territorial councils have given their approval by resolution of the territorial council of the Yukon and, I understand, by consensus of members of the territorial council of the Northwest Territories. That is the situation with regard to these parks. If this legislation is passed, these areas will become parks within the provisions of the act as it emerges from this House. As far as I can understand this amendment, if we adopt it, the minister will be obliged to consult with the councils of the territories with regard to how he goes about developing those parks. In this regard, I submit that the councils of the territories will, in fact, be on all fours with the legislatures and governments of the provinces.
Even though the law does not state that the minister has to consult with the provincial authorities, this kind of consultation does take place. In effect, what we are doing is tying the minister down to consulting with the territorial councils on the development of those parks. That is what I understand the law will mean when it is passed. The present minister, or any future minister responsible for the establishment of national parks, in Canada, would be stupid to establish a park in either of the territories

without the prior approval of the two councils. In fact, I would be happy if it were possible to have that provision in the law. When arguing the bill in the other place, the minister almost invited us to consider this aspect of the matter. It will be interesting to hear his views in committee on the bill to amend the territorial act. We can discuss that question there. Obviously, we cannot at this time tie down the question of prior approval in the parks act.
Having tried to consider what the law will mean, I am satisfied at this point that if it means the withdrawal of the proposal I made in committee, I am prepared to accept this proposal that the consultation that will be required in the development of those parks is really what is essential. However, I am not in any way retracting anything I said in committee about the need for the approval of the territorial councils to be obtained in the establishment of the parks.
In point of fact, the minister did obtain that approval, even though I might agree with the hon. member for Rocky Mountain that some of the proper hearings that should have taken place with regard to those proposals did not take place. Nevertheless, the council did approve the establishment of these parks. In that sense, let me close by saying there is some validity to the argument that the words "approval of" would be redundant in connection with this particular clause of the bill.
