speechtext:
that Bill C-105, to amend the Canada Elections Act (leave of absence) be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the aim of this bill is simply to make every Canadian eligible to be a candidate for election to Parliament to a degree not presently enjoyed. It is true that every Canadian citizen has the legal right to stand for parliament and, if elected, to serve in it. However, it is not true that every Canadian has the economic possibility of doing so because there are many Canadians who are prevented by the conditions of their work from utilizing to the full the opportunity which they are given in political theory. The purport of this bill is to make it

April 4, 1974
Canada Elections Act
possible for any Canadian who is working for a corporation, an institution, or is employed in some other way, to be eligible to stand for parliament and to serve in it without jeopardizing his own and his family's economic future.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO GRANT LEAVE OF ABSENCE TO CANDIDATE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO GRANT LEAVE OF ABSENCE TO CANDIDATE
speechtext:
The need for this provision, and the practicality of it, has been illustrated in the report of an organization called The Conference Board, an American group which recently did a study on policies on leaves for political and social action. They took a survey of 800 of the
1,000	companies studied by Fortune magazine. To this survey, 34 per cent responded, of which 28 per cent indicated they had formal policies on leaves of absence. In the report that they published they indicated the following reasons for having such a policy of providing leaves of absence so that employees might be elected to public office or in another way serve the community: first, to demonstrate corporate responsibility. A company and an institution have a certain kind of citizenship and they can be either responsible or irresponsible corporate citizens. A company that wants to indicate that it is taking a responsible part in the life of the country will surely make it possible for its employees to have the freedom to be candidates and to be members.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO GRANT LEAVE OF ABSENCE TO CANDIDATE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO GRANT LEAVE OF ABSENCE TO CANDIDATE
speechtext:
The second reason was that the corporation recognized that democracy does not function well unless all segments of the population are represented. It is, therefore, desirable that the widest possible representation of the labour force be found in the House of Commons. Third, it was recognized by the companies which have this kind of leaves of absence policy that, to a large degree, the well-being of business depends upon the kind of government that a nation has. It was said once by a corporate leader in the United States that what is good for business is good for the nation. But I think that increasingly we recognize that what is good for the nation is also good fur business.
Finally, the point was made that an opportunity for employees to participate in the political life of the country is in itself a form of job enrichment, that today we are seeing we must have a wider definition of work. Work includes not only that for which we are paid; it includes also opportunities for serving society, and one ought to see the opportunity of serving in parliament as an extension of his daily work.
I hope that it will be possible for parliament to give second reading to this bill, and to send it to committee, so that we might think in terms of it becoming the practice in Canada that all employers will be required to give to their employees a leave of absence if they become candidates for parliament, and a leave of absence should the person be elected, so that the person might then be free to serve without economic anxiety.
I could suggest to you, sir, certain precise advantages to the employee affected were this to become the common practice in Canada. First of all, it guarantees to him the record of continuous service which is necessary for most pension plans and other benefit programs. Second, and

more important, it would provide the employee with job security. One of the things that we need to make it possible for working people to seek public office is to remove the financial anxiety which now haunts so many political candidates, to make it possible for a candidate to stand for office and to serve a term here knowing that if, at the end of that term, he decides to return to industry or business or if he is defeated in the next election, at least he has a job to which to return.
There are many members in this parliament who, because of the nature of their work, are self-employed. They are able, as it were, to suspend many of their activities and their self-employment through their profession or privately owned business. They know they can go back to that activity and they enter into politics with a sense of security and family responsibility. But let us think of the large number of people who are prevented from offering themselves for public service simply because they lack that security. Can we not by this simple action make it possible to open the door of opportunity to serve in public service to a much larger number of Canadians?
I think the need for this is illustrated in the very membership of the House of Commons. I think it is fair to say that more than 50 per cent of members of parliament are self employed. As I look over the number of occupations represented in parliament I am impressed, not only by the rich diversity, but also by the way in which certain occupations are much more largely represented than others. There are 20 businessmen, two contractors, one druggist, 18 farmers, 5 industrialists, 63 lawyers, 13 merchants, 1 notary, 1 osteopath, 2 ranchers, 7 doctors, 2 veterinarians and 3 publishers, for a total of 148.
Probably most members of parliament are self-employed or in occupations and professions in which they would find it relatively easy to become self employed. I do not mean that their businesses or professions are in any way easy but it is certainly easy to become self employed if you are a member of a profession or experienced in business.
So I put it to you that we should think more in terms of parliament representing Canada as it is, and Canada is certainly not a country where 50 per cent of the people are self employed but rather, most Canadians are working for a corporation, a small business or an institution. I think that if most Canadians are to have a chance to stand for parliament and seek public office, they must have this kind of opportunity.
I think there are two important precedents that give support to the bill before us. The first of these was legislation passed in 1942 by the parliament of Canada called the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act. It was a forward looking measure that anticipated the economic insecurity forced upon a large number of Canadians who had volunteered for armed service and who, in many instances, had no guarantee that when they came back from service overseas or from another part of Canada they would have a job to return to.
Some companies, in a spirit of patriotism and social responsibility, had made that kind of guarantee, but not all employers had made it. So in 1942 parliament passed the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act which required all employers to reinstate in employment any member of His Majesty's forces who was employed before
April 4, 1974

going on active service. If we could do that for armed service, in time of war, why can we not do it for public service in time of peace? If it was right then, it is right now. We could do it then, so let us do it now.
The second precedent that gives support to my proposal is the Quebec Elections Act which in two instances accepts the principle that this bill, C-105, enunciates. I think the national assembly of Quebec has taken a forward step in this regard. The Quebec Elections Act requires, in respect to election officers, that an employer is required to allow any employee to be an election officer and to give him time off from work, and is forbidden to dismiss him on that account. Section 142a of the same act provides that every employer whose employee is a candidate must allow the employee to absent himself until the day following polling day; the employer is forbidden to dismiss him on that account, and does not have to pay him. The act provides penalties for any employer in the province of Quebec who does not comply with this provision; he must make it possible for an employee to be an elections officer or a candidate, if the employee has requested time off from his duties, without jeopardizing his future. If we extend that principle to cover the time off work that would be required for persons to serve at least one term in parliament, then we would achieve an objective which, I submit, would be welcomed across the country, one that would make it possible for Canadians to realize their aspirations.
We do not need to have any serious apprehensions about creating difficulty for an employer. For one thing, if this bill were enacted it would affect only those Canadians who are seeking public office, and that number is never enormous. In any case, it would affect most of all those who become candidates for the major political parties; consequently, we are only thinking of about 1,000 candidates every four years or so. As well, we are thinking in terms of a fraction of the 264 persons elected to parliament because there would always be a significant number of members who would be self-employed. We are thinking of a small and manageable number who would be able to contribute to the well-being of their country.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would refer hon. members to "The Great Canadian Stampede", by Alan Heisey. I think we can take his words very seriously in light of this problem. A little more than ten years ago the writer considered offering himself as a candidate for parliament and was challenged by his employer. He had to make a snap decision whether he would go ahead with his ambition to serve the people of Canada, and jeopardize his future and risk his family's security, or back off. At page 104 of his book he writes:
Before citizens can play larger roles in the political process there needs to be a clearer authority for such activities. Large corporations often discourage their employees from taking an interest in public life...
. . . we need . .. clarification in every jurisdiction of the right to elected office. Only if you have been faced with a weekend to decide between withdrawing from a commitment to public office or facing instant dismissal from your employer, can you fully share the sense of need.
That is one voice from a fellow citizen outside this chamber. Let us listen to that voice, let us recognize
Canada Elections Act
realistically that his view is shared by a large number of people, and let us do something about it. This bill gives us such an opportunity, and I hope members from all parties will join in making it possible for the bill to stay alive in order that it may go to committee for further study and, hopefully, at a later date become part of the law and the practice of this land.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO GRANT LEAVE OF ABSENCE TO CANDIDATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to speak on this bill this afternoon, because it is not a bill that we would look at in a partisan way but one that should concern us all as individual parliamentarians or citizens. I am sure there are few of us who did not have a great deal of concern, when we decided to seek public office at the federal level, about giving up a profession or a job often in the most productive years, to devote ourselves full-time to being an MP. We must all have wondered what would happen when we tried to re-establish ourselves in our professions or jobs after a period of time.
I compliment the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Stackhouse) for bringing forward Bill C-105 to amend the Canada Elections Act. The bill introduced by the hon. member and given first reading on March 18, 1974, proposes to provide to employees to whom the Canada Labour Code, part III, is applicable, leave of absence, with or without pay, to seek nomination. It would also require an employer to grant an employee elected as a member of the House of Commons leave of absence, without pay, for up to and including five years.
In any democratic jurisdiction it is recognized that it is the duty of every qualified citizen to participate in the political process of the nation and, should he aspire to being a candidate for election, that the restrictions of his employment should, in so far as reasonably possible, be removed to permit him to exercise this civic duty. This, in essence, is the provision of section 23(14) of the Canada Elections Act and is reflected for the public sector employment in section 32(3) of the Public Service Employment Act, recognizing that such action by the employee should not prejudice his continued usefulness to the public service. This provision is a natural consequence of protecting employees who wish not to sever their public service employment in the event they are unsuccessful in being elected and to ensure that the public service retains its politically neutral character.
Under the PSEA a public servant, if elected, ceases to be an employee of the public service. Bill C-105 would require employers to grant leave of absence, without pay, to an employee elected to the House of Commons, for up to five years. The rationale of this provision is to provide security to the employee to return to his former employment, should he so elect, after one tour of duty as it were, in the House of Commons.
The motives behind this provision are commendable, to a point. While the number of persons taking advantage of such a provision would no doubt be small, the impact on the employer either in the public or the private sector should be examined to determine whether such a provision is fair to an employer. It should be noted, of course, that in most cases federal jurisdiction in labour matters relates to large corporations: banks, railways, shipping companies, airlines and other national corporations. Usu-

April 4, 1974
Canada Elections Act
ally we are not considering the small employer, the employer who hires two or three people. I think that the heavy financial burden involved in this proposal would weigh heavily upon an employer who is without considerable financial means. In addition, we should consider the possible effects on the employee if he should wish to take advantage of such a provision were this amendment to become a reality.
In the past, such provisions have been brought in on a fairly large scale, in the event of a major conflict, as an incentive to providing the necessary manpower to achieve mobilization plans. Employers undertook to respect the spirit as well as the letter of such provisions as their contribution to the nation at a time when its existence was threatened. This aspect of employment security has not been considered necessary at times other than of national emergency. This bill seeks, for a very small group, special provisions for such security up to five years. Such security has been recognized to a degree by providing legislation to ensure a pension to any member of the House who has served in more than two parliaments.
One must consider the position of the employer in the private sector who would be required to rehire the employee, without notice, at any time up to the five-year anniversary date. The bill does not refer to the type of employment or level which upon return the employee would expect. In certain cases his seniority might be respected, whereas in others, especially where the absence had been for some time, one can anticipate that circumstances would have altered to the point that the rehiring would cause embarrassment to both employer and employee.
Turning to the public sector-as I see it, this provision would apply to Crown corporations-similar embarrassment could result for both employer and employee. As mentioned earlier, the Public Service Employment Act makes no such provision for extended leave of absence, and we believe that none should be considered if it is intended that we continue to respect the character of a politically neutral public service. I believe the committee must examine this aspect of the question. If someone has been active in the House of Commons in a partisan way- and we must be partisan if we are properly to carry out our function-can that person, if he is again employed in the public service, assume the degree of political neutrality which we expect of our public servants?
We must also remember that this legislation would affect only a small part of the labour force. I do not say that we should not pass this bill because it affects only a small number of people, but we must recognize that only about 6 per cent of all employees in the nation are covered by federal jurisdiction respecting employment. Those coming under provincial jurisdiction would not be included. As I understand it, this measure would not apply to persons of federal civil service status. This is another aspect which we must examine.
Is it desirable for people to play a politically partisan role and at the end of five years return to the public service: would not the political neutrality of such a person be destroyed? I think most members will recall the case

which arose a couple of years ago of the public servant who wished to be nominated. The request was refused. In the case in question the public servant played a special role requiring a high degree of independence. We must consider the many aspects of this bill. We are all concerned about the heavy responsibilities members of parliament must assume personally, and about the loss they must suffer through not following their careers or professions during time spent in the service of the House.
I want this bill to be examined by the committee. Let it be examined objectively by members of parliament who could be much affected by it. We must be cognizant of the heavy workload of the committee in connection with the electoral boundaries readjustment references now before it. Although that work must be done, I am confident that this bill will receive some consideration in the committee. Having said those few words, Mr. Speaker, I will sit down and allow other hon. members to speak.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO GRANT LEAVE OF ABSENCE TO CANDIDATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity of saying a few words on the bill before us. I am pleased, also, the party opposite will allow this bill to go to committee. I hope it will not be held up for long in committee. My party has always believed in giving individuals the freedom to run for political office. Quite a few provincial governments support the concept of leave of absence for persons who want to run for political office at the federal, provincial or municipal level. I myself was fortunate in being granted leave of absence on a year to year basis for as long as I need it. Mine is a very broadminded school board. I know of other teachers who have become members of this House but who were not able to obtain leave of absence. Clearly, there is no equality of opportunity for people to become members of this House.
I support the principle of this bill and would go even further than it does and extend the term contemplated to ten years or even for an indefinite time. Some employers are already doing this. I know that in the past some employers have harassed employees of a different political stripe who wanted to stand for nomination. A couple of years ago a story appeared in the daily newspapers of my home province concerning a chap in Vancouver who wanted to run for the NDP. His employer, obviously of a different political stripe, denied the employee, who was an executive in a small corporation, the right to be nominated. In the end, bowing to pressure exerted on him the would-be candidate withdrew. That does not speak well of our democracy.
When I was first nominated in 1968 I applied for leave of absence. My school board granted me eight weeks leave of absence without pay. Several weeks later I heard that my school board had been called by some political hatchet man who had asked, "Can Nesdoly remain as school principal if he loses the election, in view of his political beliefs?" This is the sort of thing that people in my party and, I am sure, those in other parties have had to face on occasion.
If we really believe in practising democracy we should bring forth legislation that will protect the rights of people who run for office, if they so desire. On that note I
April 4, 1974

will resume my seat and give other members a chance to say a few words. Or perhaps we could give this bill second reading now.

I wish to say seriously, however, that I am pleased the minister has agreed, in effect, to endorse this proposal of mine. In some respects I consider it to be the most significant of the changes which are being made in the original draft of the bill which, as hon. members will recall, we received from the other place. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, after much discussion in the committee I feel that a proper recognition of the rights of the Indian and other native peoples of Canada to be able, with some degree of equality, to negotiate a settlement is as well embodied in this amendment as in any measure that has come before this House.
As hon. members know, there are certain parts of Canada where no settlement by treaty or in any other form has yet been reached regarding what is sometimes referred to as native title. One of the areas of Canada where this is true to a great degree is the province of British Columbia, from which I come as a member of this House. But the same is also true of almost the entire area of the two territories. This is a situation that I think it is incumbent upon the House to consider, particularly in view of the existing constitutional structure which, for the time being at least, leaves the entire authority vested in the Crown, being the responsibility in this instance of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien).
To me, Mr. Speaker, this amendment and its passage have an importance in the context of our situation in Canada today which overrides almost any other consideration in relation to the withdrawal from normal exploitation of any lands in the territories. The amendment was originally proposed by myself in committee but was not, like certain other of my amendments, accepted. I therefore put it on the order paper, originally in the last session, for debate at the report stage without any foreknowledge whether it would receive support from any quarter of the House other than the caucus of which I am a member. I am hopeful that it will receive the unanimous endorsation of the House despite the fact that it replaces, in effect, an amendment which was moved before the committee by members of the official opposition and which, I may say at once, I did support in the form in which it was presented because at that point, as I have often had to do, I took the position that a half a loaf or a quarter of a loaf was better than none.
In view of some references, oblique and otherwise, that have been made during the course of this report stage
April 4, 1974

discussion as to whether or not I have changed my mind on certain matters, I think I should take a moment to outline the situation that has led up to our dealing with this amendment in this particular form tonight. As members of the House will recall, the committee travelled to the capital of the Yukon territory, Whitehorse, not under an order of reference dealing with this bill but under a reference of the annual report of the department. The committee heard representations in Whitehorse from quite a large number of the citizens of the Yukon territory on a variety of subjects. Because this bill was technically in the hands of the committee at that point, many of the representations that we received tended to centre upon this bill and its implications.
I think it is fair to say that as we listened to the representations that were made in Whitehorse great interest was shown about the Kluane park in the Yukon territory. While there was not what I would call unanimous support for the establishment of the park, I think there was general endorsation of the idea of a national park in the Yukon territory. In fact, as far as there was a representative voice of the Yukon in the form of its territorial council, that council made it clear to the members of the committee that they did endorse the establishment of Kluane park.
There were some serious questions raised about what this park might do to potential hydro development. Questions were also raised about what it would do in the elimination of possible mining development. But generally speaking I think it is fair to say that the people of the Yukon were interested in, and rather excited about, the possibility of a park in that vast, rugged area of mountain wilderness that runs along the easterly side of the coastal range. I think it is fair to say that that approach was acceptable to the Indian people of the Yukon territory, both those who are registered Indians and those who are sometimes referred to as non-status Indians. But they did have one very important reservation regarding their acceptance of the idea of a park, and that was that they did not want any hard and fast boundaries drawn-in fact, they said they did not want a park established-until they had completed the negotiations which are currently in progress on their land rights.
The amendment put forward to the committee in an informal way while it was in Whitehorse contained the provision that any establishment of a park should be without prejudice to the right, title or interest of the Indian people. As far as I am concerned, the idea of that amendment was sound enough, except that in law, so far as I could see, it did not effectively protect the rights of the Indian people to negotiate. However, I initially supported the amendment even though I felt it was somewhat inadequate in its actual terms. That feeling was borne out by the representations received from the president of the Yukon Indian Brotherhood. He made very clear his concern that establishment of this park as proposed would, in effect, effectively block any possibility of Indian negotiation regarding any of the lands, right or interest that they may have within the boundaries of such a park.
The basic effect of the proposal, at least as I saw it, was that the park having been established and its boundaries set, if later on it was recognized in negotiations that even
National Parks Act
as much as one acre of land within the boundaries of the park was land that remained Indian land, then this would have meant a special act of parliament would be required to remove that one acre of land from within the boundaries of the park. This was a conundrum with which I wrestled because I was very anxious that this rather unique piece of land should receive as soon as possible the kind of protection the National Parks Act provides for certain parts of the territories in Canada. At the same time, I did not want to be a party in any way to weakening the ability of the Indian people to negotiate a fair and complete settlement.
When listening carefully to the representations put to the committee by the spokesman for the Kluane park, I became more convinced that they had some real claims that should be considered in relation to the area involved. That is why I endeavoured to present to the committee an amendment which would clearly have established the intent of parliament that this area should be included in a park reserve, while at the same time putting it under the jurisdiction of the National Parks Act rather than having it remain in a park reserve in respect of which the minister has authority at any time to change his mind and decide to pull it out of the reserve. There is nothing to prevent that.
In fact, this was the position which had existed for some time in reference to Kluane, having in mind the fact that it was not in a park reserve, but a game reserve. In attempting a reasonable reconciliation with what to me were two important considerations, I felt this proposal offered a fair solution. For that reason I am pleased that the minister has agreed to lend his support to this idea. I hope all hon. members of the House will do so. I do not think it will do any substantial damage in respect of the desires of anyone concerned with the preservation of wilderness areas in Canada, particularly the unique ones, to make them part of our parks heritage.
As one individual who spoke to the committee at Whitehorse very aptly observed, if you are thinking in terms of a wilderness park, as long as you do not do anything to it, it will not go away. Having that concept in mind, I thought that was one of the wisest things I listened to in the Yukon, and I believe the proposal before us will ensure that Kluane park is preserved as part of our wilderness heritage. I may say that similar ideas have been put forward in written representations by the Indian and Innuit peoples of the Northwest Territories in respect of the Nahanni and Baffin Island park proposals.
I have here communications from organizations of the Innuit people and the Northwest Territories Indian Brotherhood that they agree with the soundness of the proposal we are discussing in this report stage amendment. I shall not take up the time of the House to detail them for the record, but I feel I should take a few minutes to draw to the attention of hon. members what I consider to be the basic importance of this report stage amendment. While I may have views that range from lukewarm to strong about some of the other issues we have been discussing, I feel the issues involved in this amendment are the most important in relation to what in all fairness we should or should not do at this point about setting aside lands which have

not been surrendered by the Indian people to the national parks system of Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words in connection with the three motions, Mr. Speaker. I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), and I gather he has changed his mind. He suggested that from the submission made to our committee the public generally in Whitehorse approved of the parks in principle, but I understood from what he said at various committee meetings that he and members of his party were concerned about public hearings in respect of parks. After listening to him tonight, I take it he feels there is no need for public hearings in respect of these parks in the territories.
Motions Nos. 6 and 8 put forth by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni have the same effect as motion No. 7, and after reading the motions I cannot help wondering why they were put forward in the first instance. Rather than setting aside lands for the Kluane and Nahanni parks, these motions would put the lands into reserves. Bill C-9, as amended in the committee, would set aside the lands as national parks, yet the effect of these three motions would simply reserve the lands. Perhaps this is a matter of semantics, but in both cases-in the original bill and in the motions as filed-the interests of the native people would be protected and in both cases the provisions of the National Parks Act would apply.
By virtue of the three amendments, the lands would be set aside simply as a reserve. In speaking on clause 10 earlier today I said that the establishment of these parks was really a fait accompli and that the matter did not require a public hearing. The parks we are concerned about, namely, Baffin Island, Kluane and Nahanni, fall into a different category than those under clause 10. In effect, the amendments put forward by the minister and by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni would preclude the possibility of public hearings in respect of these parks. I had the opportunity of attending the committee meetings at Whitehorse last fall when we heard numerous representations from people in the area in respect of Kluane park. I felt there was some opposition to the park. There were suggestions concerning alteration of the boundaries, and so on. It seemed to me there should be, under these circumstances, public hearings in order to give all interested persons an opportunity to provide input to either the committee or to the department with regard to the park.
Also during the course of our committee hearings we heard from the Innuit and native Indian association with regard to Baffin Island park. It is my opinion that in the case of the parks with which we are concerned this evening there should be public hearings and public input. It is interesting to note that under clause 10 there is reference to the Pacific Rim and four other parks. When the minister moved his motion to amend the bill he retained subclause (3) which provides:
The minister shall, at such time or times as he considers appropriate in the development of national parks in the areas described in subsection (1), hold public hearings in relation to the plans for the development of those parks.
(Mr. Barnett.]
When he came to the amendment contained in clause 11, he ignored the possibility of having public hearings with regard to the development of these three parks above the sixtieth parallel. I hope this was an oversight by the minister and I suggest that at some time in the future he bring in an amendment to the effect that when it comes to the development of these three parks above the sixtieth parallel he follow the procedure set forth under clause 10 regarding the Pacific Rim and other parks and hold public hearings to determine the feelings of the people concerning the development of the parks.
I also wonder, in respect of clause 11 which provides for 90 days' notice and publication in the Canada Gazette, why the minister retained the provision for publication in both official languages in various newspapers in Canada for four consecutive weeks, if there is no provision for public hearings to be held. I should like to know why the government would advertise in the newspapers for four consecutive weeks the intention to proclaim a park unless there were some provision to allow interested persons to provide an input. If there is no such provision, then it seems to me we are just wasting the taxpayers' money because there would not seem to be any purpose in advertising in the newspapers and saying we are proclaiming a park, if the public is to have no input. It would seem to me that if the newspapers learned that a park was to be developed, they would be happy to publish this information as a news release.
In summing up, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the minister, in respect of this particular clause, to consider in the immediate future bringing in amendments to the act so that clause 11 will be in accordance with clause 10 and will provide for public hearings on the development of parks.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the amendment before us. I wish to congratulate the minister and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) for bringing in amendments that are very similar. I understand that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has withdrawn his amendment because the two amendments aim at the same objective, which is the recognition and, hopefully, the settlement of aboriginal claims in the north. It seems to me that this is a forward step.
I suggest to the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, that similar action should be taken with respect to other lands not within park areas. Surely if we can deal with the rights of the native people in northern Canada within the confines of a national park, it makes sense that other lands should also receive similar treatment especially in view of the recent application by a consortium of 27 companies to build the Mackenzie Valley pipeline.
It would seem to me that a great many problems could be solved by the government of Canada if it would tackle the problem in a manner similar to that provided in the amendments before us tonight. I realize, as I believe every member of this House realizes, that this amendment is turning new ground so far as government is concerned. I do not think we need be too apprehensive. The natives in northern Canada have claims. These have been resisted by federal governments over the years and finally, within the last few months, we have witnessed a decision by government to recognize that some of these claims are valid and

at least should be discussed on the basis of what the natives in these areas should receive. I said earlier that is one of the reasons I certainly endorse these amendments and intend to vote for them.
While we are on the matter of national parks in the north and the rights of the native people in respect of areas which might be covered by them, there are one or two more comments I should like to make. There is no doubt that national parks, or their establishment, have been neglected over the years. National parks represent a heritage we in 1974 can leave to those who come after us. While the setting aside of great chunks of the northern territories for national park sites might seem to be excessive in light of the small number of people living in the area, nevertheless we must realize that as time goes on these will become areas of great importance. They will be wilderness parks where 50 or 100 years from now people will find out what Canada was really like. I regret deeply that more land in the southern section of Canada was not set aside for similar purposes over the years, for as time goes on we are losing some of the choicest sections of our country. Some of the rights within these areas of course have to be negotiated, whether it is north of the sixtieth parallel or in national parks' sites within the established provinces.
I do not think there is much more that I wish to say about this question, but I again urge the minister to deal with the Canadian territory north of the sixtieth degree of latitude, and I point out to him that there are other areas outside national parks which should receive attention similar to that which I hope we will take through this amendment to the National Parks Act. Again, I tell the minister that he is moving in the right direction. Although we would like to see him go a little further, we intend to support this amendment because it is good for Canada and it will, I hope, resolve one of the most serious problems facing us in the settlement of aboriginal rights in the northern part of Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on Bill C-6, particularly with regard to a very unique area, namely, the short grass area in the southern prairies. This area is unique and fragile. It is disappearing, and it offers a challenge to those who would like to see it made into a national park. Of course, the question is whether it is possible to preserve the prime ecological features of the area and still have a park for all. I must say that in my heart I have great sympathy for the minister and his endeavours in this regard. The requirements must be specific. Government authorities, federal and provincial, must operate in such a way as to keep the residents of the area closely informed of the negotiations and the consequences of those negotiations so that the full support of the people in the area may be obtained if a park is established.
There has been much opposition to the park in my area and most of the questions concerning the area between Val Marie and Killdeer in southern Saskatchewan have arisen because of the failure to make known to the ranchers in the area and to the general public answers to questions such as, why establish a park at all, and the pros and cons of establishing a national or a provincial park. People would like to know more about the actual proposed boundaries of the park and the consequences to the local inhabitants, as well as the park's attraction to the general public.
It seems only reasonable that the public, including the residents of the area, can make a wise decision on what they actually want only when they are given the factual information on which to base a decision. The government's answers that the information is confidential or that no decision has been reached have become not only frustrating but unacceptable. In his speech to the 1973 annual meeting ot the Saskatchewan Natural History Society, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) met some of the conditions required when he stated that a new national park in this or any other part of Canada must not be established to the disadvantage of local residents whose way of life depends on their traditional use of the land. So I am glad to say that if these conditions are met, there would be much less opposition to the parks, and certainly the assurance that there will be no expropriation of ranches for this Grasslands park is a "must".
The minister further stated that there will be no compulsion on ranch owners within the ultimate boundary to move. The right of the owner to pass on his land, or the right to his land to his heirs would be undisturbed, and if and when a rancher chose to sell his property, the government would be prepared to buy it at a fair market price and to offer its services to assist the rancher to relocate.
It should be possible for some historical events, such as Sitting Bull's famous rendezvous at Pinto Butte, to serve as the focus for dramatic productions, for nowhere is the campfire more characteristic than in the pages of prairie
1170

April 4, 1974
National Parks Act
history, and campfires are always welcome focal points for visiting, relaxing and learning.
Now I would like to list a short summary of negotiations between the provincial government, the federal government and municipal governments in an attempt to establish this Grasslands park in the southern area of Saskatchewan. It spans a period of over 16 years. Progress has been very slow but I think we are moving toward the establishment of a park. I must say that I was very pleased yesterday to receive a letter from the office of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, dated April 2, in which he said:
This is further to our previous correspondence about the proposed Grasslands national park in Saskatchewan.
You will be interested to know that we have recently had meetings about this on a senior level with the Saskatchewan Department of Natural Resources, and I understand that the Saskatchewan government will make a decision shortly.
I suppose it really all started in my area back in 1957 when the Saskatchewan Natural History Society introduced the idea of a Grasslands national park. Later on, in 1959, the same Saskatchewan Natural History Society passed a resolution urging the Saskatchewan government to set up a national grasslands preserve. In 1964, once again the Saskatchewan Natural History Society put forth an actual proposal for a Grasslands national park in Canada comprising some 25 townships immediately north of the U.S. border and extending from Killdeer on the east toVal Marie on the west. This area includes a diversity of habitats and scenery and contains a minimum of roads, fences and farm or ranch buildings.
Later on, in December, 1964, the Saskatchewan Stock-growers at their annual meeting discussed the possibility of a Grasslands park and expressed the hope that grazing would be allowed. This was the point which was to become a major stumbling-block over the next few years. In 1965 there was an announcement by the federal government that an attempt would be made to establish the park in Saskatchewan and once more, in April, an announcement was made by the federal government that a search for suitable areas in southern Saskatchewan was to be carried out during the summer.
The federal government, in 1966, after consideration of the previous summer's investigation, concluded that the Val Marie area appeared most suitable for the park. Some of the other areas considered were Lost Mountain Lake, Qu'Appelle Valley, Moose Mountain and Estevan. Later on, in 1966, the first sour note was revealed in a letter from Saskatchewan's public works minister who opposed the proposal. In 1967, more concern was expressed by Saskatchewan members of the legislature. The suggestions were that the prairie park be established in a province other than Saskatchewan. Then we move to 1969, with an announcement of a stalemate in negotiations between the two governments. This was the first of several that blocked progress toward the Grassland national park.
In 1970, active negotiations were reopened between the provincial and federal governments. Later on, in 1970, the federal government released a statement which said that the signing of the park agreement was little more than a formality now. They stated that all major difficulties

appeared to have been overcome. However, the provincial government replied stating that details had yet to be worked out, and the signing of the agreement was still quite far away. Still later on, in 1970, a guarantee that the grazing rights would be left or there would be no park was the crux of a statement issued by the premier of Saskatchewan. Later still, in December, a letter from the minister in Ottawa and Regina had been resolved. In 1971, the first direct contact with the ranchers occurred when members of the provincial government in Saskatchewan held a meeting in Fir Mountain, and it was here that the ranchers expressed concern over a park policy which did not allow grazing within the park.
I should like to digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker, and say that it is less than 100 years ago that a Minniconjou Sioux war party arrived in my area of southern Saskatchewan. As a matter of fact, in 1876 several lodges of Minniconjou Sioux, led by White Eagle, arrived at Wood Mountain. These Sioux had fled from Minnesota following violent conflicts with the whites over land rights. The situation grew worse when in June of the same year the Sioux, under the leadership of Crazy Horse and Sitting Bull, gathered at Little Big Horn to completely annihilate Colonel Custer and his 212 troops. The Sioux became a people on the run, turning to Canada and the Wood Mountain district for the protection of the Great White Mother. We know the rest of that story, Mr. Speaker.
Later in 1971, a liaison committee of ranchers was formed to help communications between ranchers and the government. Early in 1972, it was pointed out in Regina that if the federal government did not soon create a park, the provincial government would proceed in establishing a provincial Grasslands park. Then in May, 1972, negotiations were terminated by the provincial government when the conditions they set out appeared to be unacceptable to the federal government. In October, 1973, the federal minister announced that the federal government was willing to allow grazing rights within the park but that mineral rights would not be given up. It appeared that the federal government was willing to go halfway.
The premier of Saskatchewan stated that if grazing rights were allowed, mineral rights would be negotiable, so although there now seems to be no real obstacle to the establishment of a national Grasslands park in the Canadian plains, we cannot as yet be sure that negotiations will be completed. Developments to date have been extremely slow, but I believe that people are increasingly aware of the need for preserving samples of natural areas.
I conclude by saying that the vast grasslands are gone for ever and neither this generation nor generations to come can ever hope to replace them. But in the sparsely inhabited lands between Killdeer and Val Marie there exists a part of this vanishing legacy. I only hope that we realize in time the value of this prairie heritage, before all that remains would be the scars of technology.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by commending the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) on his remarks in this third reading debate on the amendment to the National Parks Act, and for bringing again to the attention of the House a subject which is of great concern to the southern area of Saskatchewan. This Grasslands national park, as
April 4, 1974

outlined by the hon. member, has become a controversial issue in southern Saskatchewan and I should like to touch upon some aspects of that tonight, particularly the manner in which negotiations have taken place to date.
The problem with the operation of government departments is that often one department does one thing and no other department knows what is being done. I say this to my hon. friend because while the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is seeking to establish Grasslands national park in the corner between my hon. friend's constituency and my own for the preservation of national heritage, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has signed a general agreement with the province of Saskatchewan for regional and industrial development. What kind of development do they have in mind, Mr. Speaker? The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) and I have been interested in the development on one side of the southern Saskatchewan area of a large inland lake running between Weyburn and Estevan in order to create an industrial base. Mr. Speaker, that is not entirely congruent with the development of the tourist industry.
At the other end of the constituency running into Coronach in the area where they are attempting to put the Grasslands national park, the Saskatchewan Power Corporation is carrying out an examination of the possibility of building a large hydroelectric power project. This would employ hundreds of people and maybe reduce some of the unemployment for the people of areas like Moose Jaw. That kind of development is not entirely congruent with the establishment of the Grasslands national park. There is general agreement between the province of Saskatchewan and the government of Canada. Under this agreement the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has the right to sign a subsidiary agreement. I suggest that they should do this and establish an over-all game plan for this development in southern Saskatchewan.
It is often assumed that the tourists are dragged into northern Saskatchewan where there is already a national park with lots of land, lakes, trees, etc. I submit that in southern Saskatchewan, running from Moose Mountain park through to Cypress Hills, there is real scope for the development of an alternative route to the Trans-Canada highway. If people were routed through Kenosee Lake down to Highway 13 and through the southern part of Saskatchewan, perhaps the Grasslands park could be developed without disrupting the livelihood of the people. We would be able to develop other aspects of the tourist industry in the area of my hon. friend, the member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, and in Assiniboia. A considerable number of French communities have settled there and have developed their culture. For instance, in the community of Willowbunch you will find a bilingual museum, some of which was built with OFY grants. You will find evidence of a marvellous history, of which most people travelling through Saskatchewan are not aware.
In the community of Flintoft you will find, unless it is torn down, evidence of the Roumanian culture of the people who settled in the area. If your game plan is to develop routes through southern Saskatchewan, you could develop an alternate route which would include cities like
National Parks Act
Moose Jaw, the areas of Swift Current-Maple Creek, Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain-to show I am not partisan- and Assiniboia.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext: That is highly unlikely.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
The hon. member thinks that my lack of partisanship is highly unusual. Speaking of the tourist business, the hon. member mentioned Sitting Bull and referred to the Sioux, the tribe which went back to the United States where many were slaughtered. Some of those people stayed in the Wood Mountain country. The Big Muddy is where the outlaws operating in the Dakotas and Montana used to hide in days when U.S. marshals wanted to bring them to law. This could be developed into a tourist attraction.
I am trying to convey to members of the House the tremendous potential there is for developing the tourist industry in southern Saskatchewan if only the correct game plan is followed. Of course, it will be difficult to develop the tourist industry if, less than 50 miles from an attraction, you allow a strip mining operation to deface the land. If strip mining is carried on, I do not care whether under a Conservative, Liberal, Socialist or Social Credit government, you had better institute a program to reclaim land. Do not leave those ugly hills, which were left in Estevan, over which when I was a kid I used to scramble. What happened was a terrible example of misuse of land after it had been strip mined. Strip mining is still going on. It is not a pretty sight. I know that water basins are formed with a view to creating an interest in fishing. I suspect that local residents mainly do the fishing. Many have been interested in seeing grassland parks established. The former member for Regina East and I have studied documents which came from the government two years ago dealing with matters which the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek dealt with in his remarks.
On the basis of recent statements made by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in Regina, I think there is a new willingness to accommodate the wishes of people who live in the south country and who are interested in preserving grassland. If the governments at Regina and Ottawa could keep open avenues of communication, I suspect the situation could improve. It will not improve if there is bungling on the part of civil servants, if one group says one thing and another something else. The main thing is that they should be interested in establishing communication.
I think hon. members of the House are interested in seeing national parks established in places like southern Saskatchewan in a way that will not be detrimental to the people of the area. There is a long history of national parks being established in a way that does not take into account the interests of local people. For instance, a national park was established in Newfoundland and the interests of the fishermen in the outports was not taken into account. Much bitterness arose as a result. Sometimes local people are bitter when young people from other parts of the country come to their national park in summer and get employment. There is bitterness when locals have not been able to obtain employment. These remarks apply to Prince Albert national park. I do not think there was any
27451-11)

April 4, 1974
National Parks Act
difficulty when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was prime minister, but there has been a lot of trouble since then.
If you want to establish a national park anywhere, you must be flexible in your approach. This government speaks of communications, of retaining the rights of farmers and ranchers to grazing, and of trying to accommodate the wishes of local communities. These things must be done if you want to establish a national park. After all, the preservation of our heritage is in the public interest; therefore, you must heed the interests of local people. They want to learn what is happening. Do not establish the park in such a way as to create suspicion and mystery. Let people know what is involved. The government must communicate, accommodate and consult if it is to meet some of the grievances of those who are affected by the establishment of national parks.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was delighted to see the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight) involved in this debate. He anticipated some of the remarks I intended to make on third reading of the bill, particularly the emphasis I would place on the necessity for consultation. I do not know if the hon. member was in the House earlier today when his party reversed itself on this issue. I am sorry the hon. gentleman did not speak earlier because, knowing his eloquence, I am sure he would have persuaded some of his wavering colleagues of the error of their ways. I refer particularly to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett). I agree that we can only meet the rapid increase in demand for national park facilities if the minister, the government as a whole and departmental officials are willing to meet with provincial governments and then take part in meaningful consultation with the people who are involved in the area.
Our purpose in establishing a national park is not suddenly, overnight, to create a new situation. Unfortunately, in most areas of Canada that opportunity no longer exists. Our purpose is to place the natural areas of Canada, which have now been clearly designated, under the federal government's national parks branch with a view to developing these areas over a reasonable period of time as typical specimens of national beauty or, in the case of an historic site, restoring its significance as an historic site.
Several members today have spoken about the prairie Grasslands park. This particular topic has been thrown about for the past 15 years. The tragedy is that, as expressed by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton), the opportunity that existed 10 or 15 years ago has now passed. There has been development in that area which makes it impossible to establish a prairie park along the lines of the initial concept. In the early negotiations for this park it was hoped that by meaningful consultation with the provinces and the people who are settled in the area it would be possible to reach agreement whereby we could have a grasslands park that would straddle the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary. It is difficult enough when Ottawa is negotiating with one province, but when you get a second province into the act you need to have the wisdom of Solomon and the sensitivity of a most polished diplomat.

speechtext:
At the moment we are running a two ring circus in northern affairs. A committee is meeting on another part of the Hill with members who are interested in northern affairs, particularly the very important question of local government and autonomy for the Yukon and Northwest Territories. I would like to be there. I am sure the minister would like to be there tonight. In fact, I just came from that committee meeting. Because the minister was not able to be present tonight, his parliamentary secretary suggested that we have an extraordinary meeting tomorrow morning so that the minister will have the opportunity of consulting, if I may use that word, the members of the committee. A situation has developed because members of parliament were able to meet with the elected representatives of both the northern territories in order to get the local viewpoint on the question of autonomy.
I shall not pursue the question of consultation and whether the vote this afternoon was for or against consultation. However, I want to make the point that as a result of the visit of the parliamentary committee to the national parks last August and again in December, members of the opposition came to the conclusion that the bill now before us does not make provision for consultation and deliberation with the people concerned in areas where national parks are proposed.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni, who concurred in our viewpoint in this regard and supported our amendments, which were reversed by the amendment introduced by the government, would agree that what we heard at Banff, Jasper, in the Northwest Territories and Whitehorse in the Yukon had a strong influence on the attitude members of the committee took in subsequent discussions on the legislation that is still before parliament. In those deliberations we discovered we were fighting a straw-man with regard to the idea that the public is against the conservation, reservation or designation of representative, substantial areas of land that would preserve our natural heritage. We discovered that the people, particularly in Banff and in the national parks which were established initially, are entirely in sympathy with the concept of the wise management of these national resources and their multiple use.
However, a problem arises when the minister refuses to listen to the legitimate requests put forward by these people and when his officials refuse to listen to legitimate representations. Some of the officials were with us, and I am sure we all came to the conclusion that as far as the support of the public is concerned, the battle has been won. This is the feeling which emerged from the friendly conversations and discussions in which we engaged.
National Parks Act
We are now considering this bill on third reading. There is not much we can do, unless we get support from the New Democratic Party, to move the government in the direction of public consultation, but I trust that when shaping future national parks hon. gentlemen opposite will think in terms of a more diversified program. National parks fall into only one of the categories required to meet the leisure time needs of a growing Canadian population. We need wilderness parks, certainly-unspoiled heritage. But we also need multipurpose parks. In addition, we need to preserve historic sites, many of which are being lost.
I remember the opposition we encountered from the party which now sits on the treasury benches when the Conservative Party had responsibility for these matters. In particular, I remember their vitriolic opposition to establishing a national park in the Yukon territory to commemorate one of the most romantic periods in Canadian history-the gold rush and the trail of '98. We faced tremendous opposition simply because we were spending comparatively small sums of money, when viewed in the light of the astronomic expenditures of the present government, in preserving historic sites which are being lost all too rapidly. That particular project is now being resurrected. However, I do not think there is one building in the Yukon which has been preserved in the interim, other than the old theatre. So we need to move rapidly.
I shall not prolong my remarks, because there are others who wish to speak and time is limited. However, I believe that in the interests of developing our parks' program I should once again say to the minister that consultation is the name of the game. He still has not been able to persuade Ontario to make available the necessary land for national park purposes. He still has to negotiate some of the master plans which have been under consideration for the past 14 years and which would restore excellence to some of the western parks such as Banff, Jasper, Prince Albert and Riding Mountain. These have developed in a diversified manner to meet a multiplicity of demands.
When these master plans are finally placed before the people in the respective provinces, I trust adequate opportunity will be given for an expression of opinion and that the wishes of those concerned are taken into account. If the minister is willing to engage in consultation at this level, I hope we can convince him that the only way in which he can move rapidly toward the establishment of the number of parks we need is by encouraging this process of consultation right across the board.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the bill to amend the National Parks Act which is now before parliament for third reading. It is important we should note the tremendous progress which has been made in the last five years. During that period, the number of national parks has grown from 18 to 28 and the amount of acreage has doubled. Only four new national parks had been created in the previous 40 years. I know that all members, those in the official opposition and in other parties, would wish to extend congratulations to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) who has carried out this magnificent program of expansion.

April 4, 1974
National Parks Act
Provinces such as Quebec and Ontario, which had not co-operated previously in establishing national parks, have now done so. Not long ago there were no national parks in Quebec: now there are two. In Ontario there were three small national parks, all of which had been established on federally-owned land. But during those five years the Pukaskwa national park was established in the area west of Wawa on the shore of Lake Superior. It is one of the most magnificent national parks anywhere in the country; its rugged grandeur should appeal to almost any eye. I had the opportunity to go there with the initial inventory team. It took us three hours to fly over this park twice, using a Twin Otter. The Trans-Canada Highway gives access to this new park. In addition, I understand three new national parks were established in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories during that five-year period.
I turn for a moment to the subject of national parks in the province of Ontario and the need for further parks in that province. The establishment of Pukaskwa park represented a real breakthrough and is greatly to the credit not only of the minister but of the Hon. Rene Brunelle who was provincial minister at that time. I should like to speak tonight about the opportunity which exists for the establishment of the next national park in Ontario. I believe it should be established on Manitoulin Island, which happens to be in the federal riding of Algoma. This is the largest fresh water island in the world. It is some 100 miles long and varies in width between four and 40 miles. It has dozens and dozens of inland lakes and is a magnificent part of this country. Recreational land opportunities there are spectacular.
It happens that on Manitoulin Island there is a large amount of property owned by the Ontario Paper Company. They have shown interest in selling it for several years. Both I and the provincial member of parliament have been trying to encourage the two levels of government to co-operate together in purchasing it. The land is owned, in the final analysis, by American interests and would therefore be a natural piece of property to repatriate and to be owned by Canada. Manitoulin Island would be a natural place to establish the next national park in Ontario.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWERS IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
I note with encouragement that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) applauds my words. This tract of land comprises 78,718 acres. There are about 57 miles of lakeshore on Lake Huron and the north channel of Lake Huron. Besides this there are miles of inland waterfront property, all of it located in Dawson and Robertson townships which are at the extreme westerly end of Manitoulin Island. There is also a great deal of property on Cockburn Island which is located about two miles west of Manitoulin Island. The largest percentage of the land on Cockburn Island is also owned by this paper company. The land was previously used for pulp and paper purposes but it is not used as much now for forestry.

One of the spectacular features of this proposal is on the north shore of Manitoulin Island, which is on the north channel of Lake Huron. It is considered the best boating area for cruising vessels in North America. People from all over eastern Canada and the United States go there to cruise. There are good boating facilities at the ports of Gore Bay, Little Current, Kagawong, and Meldrum Bay. The islands located in the north channel are often compared in beauty to those of the Greek Islands.
As I mentioned, this property has an estimated value of $5 million, but when you consider the value of the lake-shore and the recreational land available today, I think it would be a good move for the provincial and federal governments to co-operate in acquiring this property and establishing a national park. In a way they would be buying back an important, beautiful and valuable piece of Canada from foreign owners.
Access to Manitoulin Island, which would be very important to any new national park, is readily available from the Trans-Canada Highway, No. 17, utilizing Highway 68 from Espanola to Little Current. This coming summer, in the month of July, a new ferry service will be established plying between Tobermory on the Bruce peninsula to South Baymouth, Manitoulin Island. This new ferry service will cost over $9 million and represents another joint federal-provincial co-operative venture. Space for 110 cars will be available and the ferry will carry people rapidly to and from Manitoulin Island, providing much better access to central parts of southern Ontario. Likewise, there are good facilities for people coming by vessel to Manitoulin as well as by aeroplane to Gore Bay-Manitoulin federal airport. A new ferry service is being proposed from Meldrum Bay to De Tour, Michigan, which will provide ready access for visitors from the states of Ohio and Michigan who come in large numbers every summer. This access would be very important to any proposal for a new national park.
Support for the proposal to use the Ontario Paper Company property for park purposes has come from the Manitoulin Municipal Association, the Western Manitoulin Board of Trade, from the town of Gore Bay and from the economic development committee of Meldrum Bay. Recently we have received support from other members of parliament, such as the hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson). He has indicated there is real support among members from the Toronto area for more park and public recreational land easily accessible to this growing metropolitan area. This proposal would certainly be the best hedge against future needs for parkland for both central Ontario and northern Ontario. It would have important economic advantages for western Manitoulin. This area, which was at one time active in agriculture, logging and fishing, has declined in population in recent years although the opportunity for recreation there has never been better.
Therefore, I should like to compliment the minister on the progress he has made during the past five years on a national parks system. I hope he will take to heart this advice to locate a new national park on Manitoulin Island and that he will see it as an opportunity to establish an excellent new national park to serve not only the people of north and south Ontario but the rest of Canada.
April 4, 1974

Mr. Speaker, because this bill vitally affects the two northern territories in the establishment of one park in the Yukon and two parks in the Northwest Territories, I choose to speak this evening. I draw the attention of the members of the House to the fact that all afternoon and evening the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development has been considering Bill C-9, which is the principal reason that I and many other members who have been attending those committee sessions have been unable to participate in this debate. This is one more reason why standing committees should not be sitting while the House is sitting, particularly when the subject matter of a bill such as the one presently before the House conflicts directly with a kindred subject matter in a standing committee. There is no way members can split themselves into many different parts and attend to matters that vitally affect their constituencies, when this kind of programming occurs.
The first matter I want to deal with relates to the number of representations that have been received by members of the standing committee, and I presume by members of the House, from conservation and environmental organizations respecting the stance that this party took on the amendment that in committee stood in the name of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), requiring that before the establishment of any park occurred in the two northern territories, the approval of each of the two northern councils had to be sought.
Clause 2 of the bill makes it mandatory for the government not simply to seek the approval of but to seek the formal agreement of the provincial governments before any park is established or any boundaries are set. We in the two northern territories took the position that simple consultation was not enough. In 1970 when the Yukon Act was amended, the standing committee, when dealing with a provision which enabled the governor in council to dissolve the councils of the two territories prior to the expiration of the full term of four years, introduced an amendment which changed the situation of the governor in council consulting the two councils before such dissolution. Even that was distorted because the standing committee report to the House, and I can quote it almost precisely, said "where such consultation is deemed necessary or advisable". That kind of weasling wording means nothing. Now when we see a phrase such as that in clause 11 which obliges the governor in council to consult, we know it does not oblige the governor in council to do anything, such as seeking a formal agreement, so that the parks may be established in the north or altered after this so-called "consultation with".
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni and his colleagues in the committee quite rightly supported the position we took that that was not enough because it did not oblige the government to do anything of a concrete nature. What does consultation mean to this government? Surely my friends to the left have sufficient experience with the phrase "participatory democracy" as it was mouthed in 1968 to know that that kind of language means nothing. Surely they know that that kind of phrase is meaningless. The Indian people across this country have had enough experience, as a result of this participatory democracy, to
National Parks Act
realize that a phrase such as "after consultation with" means that there is a decision by the government and then they are told what the decision is. That is the process of consultation! It is in effect a fait accompli. The phrase "after consultation with" does not mean a damn thing.
Therefore, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, his colleagues and members of this party on the standing committee, realizing the failure of the government to go through this process of consultation, decided to put some teeth into this bill. We deleted the phrase "after consultation with" and required the government to seek the approval of the elected representatives of the people in our two northern territories.
That brings me to another point and I will deal with the somersault of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I am greatly disappointed by the completeness with which that hon. member is able to swallow himself on many occasions.

We have seen an attack on two members of our party by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). I want to tell this House and the people of Canada that these members have worked more for the ecological situation and parks in Canada than any member of the Tory party. The new member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) has done a better job for the native people during his short time in this House of Commons than the member for Yukon in the entire period he has been here. There can be no doubt about that.
There is one point I should like to make to the minister before this debate closes. In speaking of national parks there is one more thing I wish to draw to his attention. I refer to the establishment of a very large number of ecological reserves from one end of Canada to the other. He knows about the activity which is going on in this field and I hope he will assist in the establishment of these reserves which could be used for research purposes in the years to come.
I see it is ten o'clock. There are other things I should like to say, but we will abide by the commitment to let the bill pass.
